summary: Describes crankback signaling for MPLS and GMPLS RSVP-TE. When path setup is blocked because routing information is out of date, failure details are returned from the point of failure so a new attempt can avoid it. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS routers set up label switched paths using information about the network that can be out of date, so a setup request can hit a link or node that has no room left. This document adds the reporting that lets the router which sent the request learn exactly where it was blocked, so it can try again on a path that avoids that place.

subtitle: How a blocked MPLS or GMPLS path setup reports where it failed, so the next attempt can steer around the problem.

tldr.problem: Routing information used to compute a path can be out of date, so a label switched path setup request may hit a link or node without enough resources and be abandoned.
tldr.mechanism: The setup request carries re-routing flags that say who may retry, and the node that detects the failure returns an error with extra TLVs naming the blocked node, link or area so a repair point can compute a detour.
tldr.outcome: Setup and recovery ratios for LSPs can improve, especially when many setup requests are triggered at once. It is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: TLV padding
facts.value: Zero-padded to a multiple of four octets

today: RFC 4920 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It still defines the crankback TLVs and re-routing flags for RSVP-TE and GMPLS signaling.

sections.title: Background: Why a Setup Request Gets Blocked
sections.content:
RSVP-TE, the RSVP extensions for label switched path tunnels in RFC 3209, establishes explicitly routed LSPs in an MPLS network. Resources can also be reserved along a path to guarantee or control quality of service for the traffic the LSP carries. To designate an explicit path that satisfies quality of service guarantees, it is necessary to know the resources available to each link or node, and routing protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS can be extended to distribute that additional state information.

Explicit paths are computed from the distributed information held by the ingress label switching router and signaled as Explicit Routes during the setup. Explicit Routes may contain loose hops and abstract nodes, which convey routing through a collection of nodes, and this mechanism can devolve part of the path computation to intermediate nodes such as area border routers.

In a distributed routing environment, the resource information used to compute a constraint-based path may be out of date, so a setup request can be blocked because a link or node along the selected path has insufficient resources. In RSVP-TE a blocked setup can result in a PathErr message sent to the ingress or a ResvErr sent to the egress, and those messages can end the setup attempt. In Generalized MPLS, as described in RFC 3473, the Notify message can also be used to expedite notification of failures of existing LSPs to the ingress and egress routers, or to a specific repair point, which is an LSR responsible for performing protection or restoration. These mechanisms give some information about the path of the failed LSP, but not always enough to route around the problem.

Generalized MPLS extends MPLS into networks that manage layer 2, TDM and lambda resources as well as packet resources, so crankback is useful there too. In a network without wavelength converters, setup requests are likely to be blocked more often, because the same wavelength must be allocated at each optical cross-connect along an end-to-end explicit path.
sections.plainLanguage: A router computes a path for a label switched path from state it learned from OSPF or IS-IS, and that state can be stale. When the setup then fails because a link or node is full, RSVP normally returns a plain error and the setup is abandoned. Crankback makes the error carry the location of the blockage.

sections.title: Why the Re-Routing Decision Must Be Explicit
sections.content:
There have been problems in service provider networks when re-routing was inferred from indirect information. This document proposes the use of an explicit re-routing indication that authorizes re-routing, and contrasts it with the inferred or implicit indication used before.

Various existing protocol options and exchanges, including the error values of the PathErr message and the Notify message, allow an implementation to infer a situation where re-routing can be performed. That inference is not always desirable, because it may be doomed to failure. The document notes that experience with release messages in TDM-based networks, for analogous implicit and explicit re-routing purposes, gives some guidance, and puts that background in Appendix A.

With topology information distribution, as performed by routing protocols such as OSPF, the ingress LSR could infer the re-routing condition. Convergence of topology information using routing protocols is typically slower than the expected LSP setup times, however. One of the reasons for crankback is to avoid the overhead of available-link-bandwidth flooding, and to use local state information more efficiently to direct alternate routing to the path computation point. The document also notes that an event-dependent routing scheme can use crankback alone, without available-link-bandwidth flooding, to decide the re-route path through learning models, and that reducing that flooding reduces overhead and may make much larger autonomous systems possible.

For these reasons the use of alternate routing should be based on an explicit indication, and it is best to know two things separately: where the blockage or congestion occurred, and whether alternate routing should be attempted at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The document insists that the decision to try again is made explicitly, by a flag on the request, rather than guessed from the error. The reason is practical: a retry that is guessed at can fail again, and the topology information converges more slowly than the setup attempts do.

sections.title: Required Operation: Finding and Avoiding the Blockage
sections.content:
When an LSP setup request is blocked because resources are unavailable, an error message response carrying the location identifier of the blockage should be returned to the LSR that initiated the setup, which may be the ingress LSR, the area border LSR, the AS border LSR or some other repair point. The error message carries an error specification that indicates the cause of the error and the node or link on which it occurred. Crankback operation may require further information than that.

A repair point that receives crankback information resulting from the failure of an established LSP may apply local policy to govern how it attempts repair. It may prioritize repair attempts between several failed LSPs, and it may treat LSPs that have been locally repaired as less urgent candidates for end-to-end repair. Other LSRs may be repairing LSPs affected by the same fault, so an LSR may stagger its repair attempts to reduce the chance of resource contention.

Computing an alternate path depends on where the repair point sits. In a flat network without partitioning of the routing topology, the ingress LSR computes an alternate path around the blocked link or node to satisfy the quality of service guarantees, using link state information about the network, and sends a new LSP setup request over that path. In a network partitioned into areas, the area border LSR may intercept and terminate the error response and perform alternate routing within the downstream area. In a third scenario any node within an area may act as a repair point, behaving much like an area border LSR. That is useful where domains of computation do not coincide with the routing partition boundaries, but if every node re-routes, the network and CPU resources spent on re-routing attempts would be better spent at designated re-routing nodes alone.

The information needed for re-routing is ideally the node, the link and the reason for the failure. The reason can be an important discriminator: a failure that indicates no route to destination is likely to lead to a new path computation that excludes the reporting LSR, while the reason temporary control plane congestion might lead to a simple retry after a suitable pause. Even that may not be enough. If the explicit route contains a non-explicit abstract node or a loose hop, the failed node and link do not tell the repair point which hop in the explicit route has failed, so the crankback information has to indicate where within the explicit route the problem occurred.

Once a new route is known it can be signaled as an Explicit Route. If the repair point does not have sufficient topology information to compute an Explicit Route guaranteed to avoid the failed link or node, route exclusions as defined in RFC 4874 can be used, presenting the crankback information as exclusions that force avoidance of the failed node, link or resource.

The repair point should store the location identifiers of the blockages until the LSP is established or until it abandons re-routing attempts. Because crankback information may come back more than once while a particular LSP is being set up, the repair point SHOULD maintain a history table of all experienced blockages for that LSP, so that the resulting path computations can detour around all of them. The purpose of the table is to correlate information across repeated retries: if an attempt through B fails and an attempt through C also fails, the next attempt SHOULD NOT route through B.

The history table may be discarded once the LSP is established through the repair point. If it is kept longer, it SHOULD be discarded after a local timeout, so that it is available for re-routing attempts but not applied to a later attempt to re-establish a failed LSP. It is RECOMMENDED that the timer be no larger than the LSP retry timer configured on the ingress LSR. The information in the history table is not intended to supplement the traffic engineering database used to compute paths for other LSPs.

Multiple blockages can occur for the same LSP and successive attempts can fail, so retaining the error information avoids thrashing and the knowledge of blockages grows with each attempt. If a repair point cannot compute a path that avoids all of the blockages, it must pass an error indication upstream, and it is most useful for the upstream nodes if that message identifies all the downstream blockages and also the repair point that could not compute an alternate path.

Each repair point SHOULD apply a limit to the number of attempts it makes, either per node or as a network-wide value. When the limit is exceeded the LSR reports the failure upstream until it reaches the next repair point, or the ingress, which may act as a repair point or declare the LSP failed. The reason for the limit is that endless retries add setup latency and degrade performance by increasing signaling processing and message exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: The node that detects the blockage returns an error that names the node, the link and the reason. The repair point that receives it keeps a list of every blockage seen for that path, computes a new path that avoids all of them, and gives up after a set number of attempts, passing the error further upstream.

sections.title: Controlling Who May Re-Route
sections.content:
When a request is made to set up an LSP tunnel, the ingress LSR should say whether it wants crankback information to be collected if the setup fails, and whether it requests re-routing attempts by any or by specific intermediate nodes. For this purpose a Re-routing Flag field is added to the setup request messages, and the values are mutually exclusive.

No Re-routing is the default and the backwards compatible option. The ingress node MAY attempt re-routing after the failure and intermediate nodes SHOULD NOT. Nodes detecting failures MUST report an error and MAY supply crankback information.

End-to-end Re-routing also leaves intermediate nodes out: the ingress MAY attempt re-routing, intermediate nodes SHOULD NOT, and nodes detecting failures MUST report an error and SHOULD supply crankback information.

Boundary Re-routing allows intermediate nodes to attempt re-routing only if they are Area Border Routers or AS Border Routers. The boundary router can either forward the error upstream to the ingress or try to select another egress boundary LSR, while other intermediate nodes SHOULD NOT attempt re-routing. Nodes detecting failures MUST report an error and SHOULD supply crankback information.

Segment-based Re-routing allows any node to attempt re-routing after it receives an error report and before it passes the error further upstream. Nodes detecting failures MUST report an error and SHOULD supply full crankback information.

A node that detects the failure to set up an LSP, or the failure of an established LSP, SHOULD act according to the Re-routing Flag on the request. If segment-based re-routing is allowed, or if boundary re-routing is allowed and the detecting node is an ABR or ASBR, the node MAY immediately attempt to re-route. If end-to-end re-routing is indicated, or if segment-based or boundary re-routing is allowed and the node chooses not to attempt a re-route or has exhausted its attempts, it MUST return a protocol error indication and SHOULD include full crankback information.

Each repair point SHOULD apply a locally configurable limit on the number of attempts, which prevents excessive network usage during significant faults and allows back-off to other repair points that may have a better chance of routing around the problem. An error code and value of "Routing Problem" and "Re-routing limit exceeded", written as 24/22, marks that a node has abandoned crankback re-routing because it reached its retry threshold. A node receiving that status code MAY also attempt crankback re-routing, but it is RECOMMENDED that such attempts be limited to the ingress LSR.

On the wire the choice is carried by the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object defined in RFC 4420, which is used on Path messages. Three bits are defined for the LSP Attributes TLV, with bit numbers assigned by IANA: bit 1 for end-to-end re-routing desired, bit 2 for boundary re-routing desired and bit 3 for segment-based re-routing desired.
sections.plainLanguage: Four behaviours are possible, chosen by the router that starts the setup. With no re-routing only the ingress retries. With end-to-end re-routing the ingress retries and errors carry full information. With boundary re-routing only area and AS border routers may retry inside their own area. With segment-based re-routing any node may retry its own segment. Three bits in the LSP attributes object carry the choice.

sections.title: The New TLVs
sections.content:
RFC 3473 defines an IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object that can be used on PathErr, ResvErr and Notify messages to carry the information of the Error Spec object defined in RFC 3209, and that has scope for carrying TLVs that identify the link associated with the error. The TLVs it defines are used in two places: in the IF_ID RSVP_HOP object they identify links, and in the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object they identify the failed resource, which is usually the downstream resource from the reporting node. Five TLV types already exist for this: type 1 for an IPv4 interface address, type 2 for an IPv6 interface address, type 3 for an interface index, and types 4 and 5 for component interfaces, which are obsoleted by RFC 4201 and SHOULD NOT be used to identify component interfaces in these objects.

This document defines 22 further TLV types for the same object, numbered 6 to 27. Types 6 and 7 carry the downstream and upstream GMPLS labels; types 8, 9, 10 and 11 carry the TE Router ID, the OSPF area, the IS-IS area and the autonomous system; types 12 and 13 carry the explicit route context and the next explicit route context; types 14 to 20 carry the previous hop address, the incoming interface address and index and the incoming labels; types 21 to 24 repeat the reporting node's identity and location; and types 25 to 27 carry a proposed explicit route and lists of node and link exclusions. All TLVs are zero-padded to a multiple of four octets, so a value that is not itself a multiple of four octets has to be told apart from the padding by knowledge of the context.

The value formats are given in the document. The Router ID used in types 8 and 21 is 32 bits. The OSPF area identifier in types 9 and 22 is 4 octets. The IS-IS area identifier in types 10 and 23 carries a length of the actual, non-padded identifier, with valid values from 2 to 11 octets inclusive, and is padded with trailing zeroes to a four-octet boundary. The autonomous system number in types 11 and 24 is 32 bits, and where 16-bit AS numbers are in use the low order bits, 16 through 31, carry the number while the high order bits are set to zero. The explicit route TLVs carry a sequence of Explicit Route Object subobjects. The node exclusions TLV, type 26, carries a sequence of TLVs of types 1, 2 or 8 that name downstream nodes already declared unusable, and the link exclusions TLV, type 27, carries a sequence of TLVs of types 1, 2 or 3 that name incoming interfaces at downstream nodes already declared unusable.

The document gives guidance on which TLVs to use. If crankback is not being used, inclusion of an IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object follows the processing rules of RFC 3473 and RFC 4201, and a sender MAY include TLVs of types 6 to 27 for informational and monitoring purposes. If crankback is being used, the sender MUST use the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object and MUST include at least one of the TLVs in the range 1 to 3, with additional TLVs SHOULD also be included to report further information.

The TLVs fall into three groups. The error report TLVs, types 1 to 3, are the ones that must be present. The fundamental crankback TLVs, types 1 to 11, report the specific resource that failed and SHOULD be supplied whenever the reporting node has the information, although types 8, 9, 10 and 11 MAY be omitted according to local policy and relevance. The additional crankback TLVs, types 12 to 27, help to locate the fault within the context of the path of the LSP: types 12 to 15 set the context of the error within an explicit path that has loose hops or non-precise abstract nodes, where the difference between type 12 and type 13 is the difference between the hop the node was trying to satisfy and the next hop it was trying to reach. Types 21 to 24 expand the location of the reporting node, and types 25 to 27 give extra information for recomputation points, such as lists of failed nodes and links that can also be factored into route exclusions. There is no ordering requirement on the TLVs, and no meaning should be read into the order they arrive in. All LSRs MUST be prepared to receive and forward any TLV, and an LSR that proposes to perform crankback re-routing SHOULD support receipt and processing of all the fundamental crankback TLVs and is RECOMMENDED to support the additional ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The error message carries the new information as type-length-value fields inside the IF_ID error specification object. Twenty-two new field types are defined, from 6 to 27, covering the failed interface, node, area, autonomous system, the position in the explicit route, and lists of nodes and links to exclude.

sections.title: Acting on Crankback Information
sections.content:
A node that receives crankback information in a PathErr must first check whether it is allowed to perform re-routing, which is indicated by the Re-routing Flags in the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object of the setup request. If it is not allowed, it should forward the PathErr, or, if it is the ingress, report the LSP as failed. If re-routing is allowed, it should compute a path to the destination using the original explicit path and excluding the failed or blocked node and link, add that path to a new LSP setup request as an explicit route and signal it. It should store all received crankback information for the LSP until the LSP is established or the node abandons its attempts, and should exclude everything reported by previous attempts from the next computation.

To compute an alternate path, the blocked links or nodes and their locations have to be identified. The common identifier of each link or node in an MPLS network should be specified, and both protocol-independent and protocol-dependent identifiers may be used. In link state protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS, each link and node can be uniquely identified, for example by the context of a TE Router ID and the Link ID. When routing-protocol-specific link identifiers are used, the Re-routing Flag on the setup request must have been set to show support for boundary or segment-based re-routing.

The explicit route of the original request may contain a loose hop or an abstract node, in which case the crankback information may refer to links or nodes that were not in the original explicit route. To help with this, the crankback information reports the top two hops of the explicit route as received at the reporting node: the first hop will likely identify the node or the link, and the second identifies the next hop from the original explicit route.

When a node cannot or chooses not to re-route, it must forward the PathErr further upstream. However, when a node was responsible for expanding or replacing the explicit route as the setup was processed, it MUST update the crankback information with regard to the explicit route it received, because only then can the upstream nodes route around the problem.

If a node's re-routing attempts fail, it accumulates the failure information, and when it gives up it MUST propagate the failure message further upstream and include crankback information when it does so. Passing on the full list of every failure from several repair points could lead to too much signaled information, so a compression mechanism is available in TLVs 26 and 27. Aggregation may involve reporting all links from a node as unusable, flagging an ABR as unusable when there is no downstream path available, or including a TLV of type 9, which results in the exclusion of the entire area. The precise details of aggregation are beyond the scope of the document.

Resource allocation failure in RSVP-TE can occur on the reverse path as the Resv message is processed, and the egress LSR still has the option of re-issuing the Resv with different resource requirements, though not on an alternate path. On receiving a ResvErr that carries crankback information, the egress LSR MAY ignore the object and act as it would for any other ResvErr. If it supports the crankback extensions and all its local recovery procedures have failed, it SHOULD generate a PathErr message carrying the crankback information and send it to the ingress LSR. If a ResvErr reports on more than one FILTER_SPEC, only one set of crankback information should be present and it should apply to all of them, which may mean generating more than one PathErr.

The Notify message defined in RFC 3473 enhances error reporting and is sent to the addresses requested on the Path and Resv messages, which could but need not identify the ingress and egress LSRs. An LSR that supports the crankback extensions MAY choose to send a Notify message carrying crankback information, which gives a speedier report of the error. In a network that offers crankback at several nodes, the LSRs have to agree on whether PathErr or Notify provides the stimulus for crankback, because otherwise several nodes might try to repair the same LSP at once.

A new error value is defined for the error code "Routing Problem": "Re-routing limit exceeded", which means re-routing has failed because the number of crankback attempts went beyond the predetermined threshold at an individual LSR.

Backward compatibility is a stated concern, because not every node in an RSVP-TE network will support these extensions. It is important that an LSR that does not support them can continue to process a PathErr, ResvErr or Notify message even if it carries the newly defined IF_ID ERROR_SPEC information. The document says it introduces no backward compatibility issues, provided that existing implementations conform to the TLV processing rules of RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.
sections.plainLanguage: A node that receives the error first checks whether its flag allows it to retry. If it may, it computes a path that keeps the original explicit route but excludes the failed node or link, and it excludes everything reported by earlier attempts too. If it may not, it passes the error upstream.

sections.title: LSP Recovery Considerations
sections.content:
LSP recovery recovers an established LSP when a failure occurs along the path, and the crankback extensions can be applied to improve it. The document's example covers on-demand LSP recovery, which attempts to set up a new LSP after an LSP failure is detected.

Upstream of the fault, an LSR that detects a fault on an adjacent downstream link or node sends a PathErr upstream. In GMPLS the ERROR_SPEC object may carry a Path_State_Remove_Flag indication, and each LSR receiving the message then releases the corresponding LSP; if that indication is not present, the ingress node MUST issue a PathTear so the resources are released. If the failed LSP has to be recovered at an upstream LSR, the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC that includes the location of the failed link or node is included in the PathErr message, and the ingress, the intermediate area border LSR, or any other repair point permitted by the Re-routing Flags can terminate the message and perform alternate routing.

In a flat network the ingress LSR computes an alternate path around the blocked link or node that satisfies the quality of service guarantees and sends a new Path message over it. In a network segmented into areas, the behavior follows the flags. With end-to-end re-routing the PathErr travels all the way back to the ingress LSR, which may issue a new Path message along another path. With boundary re-routing the ingress area border LSR MAY terminate the PathErr and perform alternate routing within the area for which it is the ingress LSR. With segment-based re-routing any node MAY apply those procedures.

Downstream of the fault, a node that detects a fault MAY send a PathErr or a Notify message containing an IF_ID ERROR SPEC that includes the location of the failed link or node, and MAY send a PathTear to clean up the LSP at the other downstream nodes. If the reservation style for the LSP is Shared Explicit, the detecting LSR MAY choose not to send a PathTear, which leaves the downstream LSP state in place and facilitates make-before-break repair that reuses the downstream resources. The unused state then times out according to the normal rules. A similar decision might be made at a well-known merge point such as an ABR or ASBR, where a received PathTear might be absorbed rather than propagated downstream for an LSP with a Shared Explicit reservation style, although the document notes that this is a divergence from the protocol and might severely affect the normal tear-down of LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The same reporting is used to recover an established path after a link fails. The error travels upstream to a router allowed to repair, which then sets up a new path that avoids the failed link. A node that detects the fault may also leave the downstream state in place so the new path can reuse it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RSVP-TE trust model assumes that RSVP-TE neighbors and peers trust each other to exchange legitimate and non-malicious messages, and the document says this assumption is necessary for the signaling protocol to function. The trust model is assumed to cascade, so an LSR that trusts its neighbours extends that trust to the LSRs its neighbours trust, which in practice creates a trust domain across the network. Authentication of neighbour identity is already a standard provision of RSVP-TE, as is protection of messages against tampering and spoofing, and those mechanisms apply to the hop-by-hop exchanges used for crankback propagation on PathErr messages as well as to the directed exchanges used on Notify messages. Key management may also be used to protect against impersonation and message content falsification, which requires keys to be maintained, exchanged and configured on each LSR, so it is important to limit the number of keys.

The document does not introduce any protocol elements or message exchanges that change the operation of RSVP-TE security. It does add that crankback is envisaged as an inter-domain mechanism, so crankback information is likely to be exchanged over trust domain borders. In those cases the information from inside a neighbouring domain would be of little or no value to the node performing the re-routing and would be ignored, and the reporting domain is likely to have applied some form of information aggregation to preserve the confidentiality of its network topology.

The document then describes the attacks that remain possible. A direct attack by one domain upon another is possible, and domain administrators should apply policies to protect their domains against another domain thrashing LSPs by allowing them to be set up before being reported as failed; contracts between trust domains are expected to give some protection. A more serious threat arises if a domain reports that neither it nor its downstream neighbour can provide a path to the destination, because such a report could be bogus, with the reporting domain not having given the downstream domain the chance to try. The document notes that this problem does not arise between nodes inside one domain, because of the trust model, that the behaviour is hard to overcome, and that it may be detected by sending indirect path computation requests to the falsely reported domain, using mechanisms such as the Path Computation Element in RFC 4655. A separate document describing inter-domain MPLS and GMPLS security considerations is to be produced.

Finally, the extensions introduce no new security holes in the protocols, but a malicious user who gains protocol access might use the crankback information to prevent the establishment of valid LSPs. The document therefore says the existing security features available in RSVP-TE should be considered carefully by all deployers, and SHOULD be made available by all implementations that offer crankback.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP-TE assumes that neighbouring routers trust each other, and crankback information travels with that same trust. Across domain boundaries the information is usually of no use and is ignored. A malicious domain could report failures that do not exist, so domain policies matter, and the existing RSVP-TE protections should be turned on.

viz.caption: THE FOUR RE-ROUTING BEHAVIOURS OF RFC 4920

items.label: Default
items.desc: Only the ingress node may attempt re-routing.

items.label: Bit 1
items.desc: The ingress node may re-route; intermediate nodes should not.

items.label: Bit 2
items.desc: Area border and AS border routers may re-route inside their area.

items.label: Bit 3
items.desc: Any node may re-route its own segment before passing the error on.

viz.caption: GROUPING THE CRANKBACK TLVs BY WHERE THE FAILURE IS (RFC 4920, SECTION 6.3.5)
WHAT THE CRANKBACK INFORMATION CAN CARRY

items.title: Interface
items.text: The address, index or label of the interface that failed.

items.title: Node
items.text: The router ID of the node that failed or reported the failure.

items.title: Area
items.text: The OSPF or IS-IS area in which the failure occurred.

items.title: Autonomous system
items.text: The autonomous system number of the reporting node.

items.title: Explicit route context
items.text: The hop that was being satisfied, and the next hop, inside a loose or abstract node.

items.title: Exclusions
items.text: Lists of nodes and links already found unusable, for the next computation.
